transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, it's... it's my sleep, primarily. Or rather, the complete and total lack of it. It’s become completely unmoored, just entirely untethered from any normal rhythm or routine I’ve known in my sixty-nine years. At first, you see, it felt almost... productive. I’d sleep for maybe two, perhaps three hours at the absolute most, and I’d wake up just buzzing. I’d be out of bed before the sun, drafting these incredibly complex plans—blueprints, really, for community projects, restructuring my entire financial portfolio, writing letters to local officials. I felt entirely ready to go, like I had tapped into some hidden wellspring of energy that sleep was just getting in the way of. I thought I had finally figured out how to maximize my time, especially now that I'm not working and have all these hours to fill. But now... now it’s shifted. It’s changed entirely. I’m still not sleeping, but instead of that boundless energy, I just lie there awake long before dawn. I stare at the ceiling, and my stomach is just tied in these awful, tight knots. There’s absolutely no sense of rest, no reprieve. It’s just this hollow, exhausting wakefulness, and it’s stretching on and on, night after night, until the days and nights just blur together into this one long, terrible stretch of time. I just don't know how much longer I can sustain this, to be perfectly honest with you.
Do you find yourself enjoying things you used to like, or has that changed recently?

Well, that's... that's a very good question, doctor, and honestly, it’s been one of the most distressing parts of all this. The short answer is no, not at all. But to really explain it... you see, I’ve always been a man with hobbies. Passions, really. Since I retired, I’ve had the time to really dive into them. I used to spend whole afternoons, just entire days, really, at the art museum downtown. I'd wander the galleries, study the brushstrokes... or I’d lose myself completely in my photography. I have this wonderful old Leica, and I’d spend hours setting up the perfect shot, waiting for the light to hit just right. And cooking! I used to love preparing these elaborate, multi-course meals from scratch. It was a joy, a real creative outlet for me. 

But lately... it's just gone. The desire, the pleasure, it’s completely evaporated. I look at my camera sitting there on the desk, gathering dust, or I think about going down to the community center for my regular bridge game, and I feel... absolutely nothing. It’s like a void where the enjoyment used to be. The only thing I do feel is this overwhelming sense of exhaustion at the mere thought of it. The effort it would take just to go through the motions, to sit at the bridge table and pretend to care about the cards, or to smile and make small talk with the other players... it just feels insurmountable. It's not just that I don't want to do these things, it's that the very idea of them feels heavy, like a physical weight. I used to be so engaged with the world, and now... now I just can't seem to find a reason to connect with any of it. It's quite frightening, really, to lose that part of yourself.
Do you often feel guilty or remorseful about things you've done or haven't done?

Guilty? Oh, doctor... guilt doesn't even begin to cover it. It's more like this crushing, suffocating weight of absolute worthlessness. It just sits right here on my chest, constantly. You see, during that... that period I mentioned earlier, when I was sleeping two hours a night and feeling like I could conquer the world, I made some decisions. Financial decisions. I was so certain, so utterly convinced of my own brilliance. I thought I was seeing patterns in the market that everyone else was missing. I had charts spread out all over the dining room table, color-coded, cross-referenced... I felt like a genius. 

So, I moved a significant portion of our retirement savings. A very significant portion. I put it into this venture that... well, let's just say it was highly speculative. And now... now the dust has settled, and the reality of what I've done is just staring me in the face. I keep replaying that decision in my mind, over and over, like a broken film reel. Every click of the mouse, every form I signed... I just sit there and tell myself what an absolute fool I am. For forty years, doctor, forty years I was the responsible one. I was the provider, the steady hand. I planned meticulously for our retirement so my wife wouldn't have to worry about a single thing. And in the span of a few weeks, I jeopardized all of it. I look at her across the breakfast table, and she doesn't even know the full extent of it yet, and I just feel this sickening wave of remorse. I've ruined her security. I've taken the safety net we spent a lifetime weaving and just... set a match to it. How do you forgive yourself for something like that? How do you even look in the mirror when you know you've been so incredibly reckless, so stupid? I just... I can't stop thinking about what a profound failure I've become in the twilight of my life.
How long have you been feeling this overwhelming sense of worthlessness and lack of enjoyment in activities?

Well, let me think back... it's hard to keep track of time when the days are just this gray slog, you know? But if I really piece it together, this... this heavy, awful feeling, the guilt, the complete withdrawal from everything I used to love... it's been going on for about nine months now. Yes, nine months. It started right after everything with those financial plans fell apart. 

I remember it vividly, actually. It was late autumn. The leaves were just starting to turn, and I had been so high on my own supposed brilliance, so sure that I was securing this incredible future for us. And then the first statement came in. I remember sitting at my desk—the same desk where my camera now sits gathering dust—and opening that envelope. It was like all the air was sucked out of the room. The numbers were just... devastating. And it wasn't just a bad day in the market, it was the realization that the entire foundation of my strategy was flawed. I had been completely delusional. 

That was the turning point, doctor. Right then and there, the energy, the grand ideas, the feeling of being invincible—it all just vanished, like a switch had been flipped. And in its place, this... this crushing weight settled over me. It started as panic, but it quickly hardened into this deep, immovable sense of failure. Nine months of waking up long before dawn, staring at the ceiling, and just letting the guilt wash over me. Nine months of not touching my camera, not going to the museum, not even being able to stomach the thought of playing bridge with the neighbors. It feels like a lifetime, honestly. I keep waiting to wake up and feel like myself again, like the man who planned carefully and enjoyed his life, but every day it's just the same hollow, guilty existence. Nine months of just... existing in this dark place.
Have you experienced any thoughts or beliefs that seem unreal or detached from reality during this time?

Detached from reality? No... no, doctor, actually, that's... that's the great irony of all this. The absolute tragedy of it, really. I almost wish I were detached from reality. I truly do. If I could just float away into some... some fantasy world where none of this happened, where the money was still in the bank and my retirement was still secure, maybe it wouldn't hurt so much. But no, my mind is entirely, painfully rooted in the facts. 

I don't hear voices, if that's what you're getting at. I don't see things that aren't there, and I don't have any bizarre theories or... or strange beliefs about people being out to get me or anything like that. The reality I'm living in is just the one I created. It's the bank statements. It's the exact, precise dollar amounts I lost. I know exactly what day it is, I know exactly where I am, and I know exactly how much I've failed my wife. 

I sit in my study, and I look at the walls, and everything is exactly as it is. There's no distortion at all. Just... clarity. A terrible, punishing clarity. Now, you could argue that during that time I was up, when I was trading and sleeping two hours a night... maybe then my beliefs were a bit detached, thinking I was some sort of undiscovered financial savant. But during these last nine months? In this dark place? No. It's all too real. Every single agonizing second of it is just the plain, unvarnished truth of my own foolishness. There's no escape into unreality for me, doctor. Just the cold, hard facts.
Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself during this difficult time?

Harming myself? Oh, doctor... it's... it's a terrifying place to find your own mind wandering into. I never thought I'd be the kind of person to entertain such things. For sixty-nine years, I've been the one holding everything together, the one who planned, the one who persevered. But these last nine months... the weight of it all, the sheer, unadulterated guilt of what I've done to our life savings... it wears you down in a way I can't even begin to properly articulate. 

It's not that I sit there planning it out with a notepad, but... well, there are mornings—far too many mornings lately—when I open my eyes, and before I even fully register the sunlight coming through the blinds, that crushing realization hits me again. And in that split second, I just think... it would be such a profound relief if I simply did not wake up. If I could just slip away quietly and not have to face the day, not have to look at my wife and know I've ruined her twilight years. It feels like slipping away would be a kindness to both of us, honestly. 

And it... it escalated a bit recently. It got to a point where the thoughts were just so loud, so persistent, circling around and around in my head like vultures. I was sitting in my study, looking at the letter opener on my desk, and my mind just went to this very dark, very frightening place. It scared me, doctor. It really did. It scared me so much that I actually broke down and told my wife. I told her... I told her she shouldn't leave me alone right now. I couldn't bear the thought of what I might do if I were left to my own devices with these thoughts. So yes, the thoughts are there, and they are... they are deeply, deeply unsettling.
Would you say your feelings of worthlessness and guilt are present most of the day or nearly every day?

Oh, every single day, doctor. Every day, all day. From the moment I open my eyes until I finally manage to drift off... and honestly, even then, it bleeds into my dreams. It is a constant, suffocating presence. 

I just... I sit in that leather chair in my study, the one by the window where I used to read the morning paper and feel so accomplished, and I just keep replaying it. Over and over and over again. Every single step of that disastrous investment decision. I think about the articles I read, the financial models I built—oh, the spreadsheets, I spent hours on them, color-coding the projections, thinking I was so incredibly brilliant—and I just replay the exact moment I authorized the transfer of our funds. The exact click of the mouse. 

And I sit there, for hours on end, and I just tell myself that I have completely, irrevocably ruined my wife’s security. She trusted me, you see. For over forty years, she never had to worry about a single bill. I was always the one who handled the accounts, the one who made sure the mortgage was paid, the one who carefully built up our nest egg so we could have a comfortable, dignified retirement. I was always the responsible one. A lifetime, doctor! A literal lifetime of being the steady, reliable man, the one our friends would actually come to for advice on their own portfolios. 

And then I just threw it all away. I made an absolute fool of myself. A complete and utter fool. And it's not just a passing thought, it doesn't just come and go. It's a physical weight. It sits right here on my chest, this agonizing guilt, because I look at her when she brings me a cup of tea, and she smiles at me with so much patience, and all I can think is, "I've destroyed your future." She should be planning those river cruises we talked about, or looking at remodeling the kitchen like she always wanted, but instead, I've left us with this catastrophic mess because of my own unbelievable hubris. 

So, yes, to answer your question, it is most of the day. It is nearly every second of every day. I cannot escape the loop of it. I just sit there replaying it, agonizing over how I took a lifetime of careful, responsible planning and just... just set it on fire. It never stops playing in my head.
How long have you been feeling this way, with the lack of enjoyment in activities and the overwhelming sense of worthlessness?

Well, doctor, it's... it's been about nine months now. Nine incredibly long, agonizing months. It all really started when... when the reality of what I had done finally set in, when those grand, foolish plans of mine completely fell apart. 

You see, before that, I was so sure of everything. I was so incredibly confident, riding high on this... this absolute certainty that I was making the smartest move of my life. But then the market shifted, the numbers started coming in, and the whole house of cards just collapsed. And right then, right when I saw the final balance, it was like a switch flipped. It was almost instantaneous. The energy, the drive, the absolute conviction I had—it just vanished, completely evaporated. 

And ever since that day, for these past nine months, it's just been this... this low, grinding withdrawal from everything. I haven't picked up a book, I haven't gone to my golf club, I haven't even wanted to tend to the garden, which I used to love. The roses are probably dying out there, and I just can't bring myself to care. All I can do is sit in my study, completely consumed by this... this overwhelming, paralyzing guilt. It's been nine months of just sitting there, withdrawing from my wife, from my friends, from my entire life, just replaying the disaster over and over. So yes, it's been about nine months since the bottom fell out, and I haven't known a single moment of peace or enjoyment since.
Would you describe your current feelings of worthlessness and guilt as being moderately severe or extremely severe?

Extremely severe, doctor. I... I honestly don't think there's a word strong enough for it, but yes, extremely severe. It's not just a feeling, you see, it's... it's an absolute conviction that I have destroyed everything of value in my life. 

I know I've mentioned it already, but I just can't stop the loop in my head. I sit there and I keep replaying that investment decision. Every single detail of it. I see the screens, I remember the exact reasoning I used, the absolute arrogance I had when I made the transfers... and I just keep telling myself, over and over, that I have completely ruined my wife's security. I look at her and the guilt is so profound it actually makes me physically nauseous. 

For my entire life—my entire adult life—I was the responsible one. I was the one who managed the money, the one who planned for the future, the one everyone looked up to as a model of stability. I went to graduate school, I built a career, I did everything right. And then... to just make such a colossal fool of myself, to throw away a lifetime of being the steady hand at the wheel... it's unbearable. The guilt is... it's monumental. It's a crushing, suffocating weight that never, ever lifts. So yes, extremely severe doesn't even begin to cover the depth of it, but it's the closest description I can give you.
Are there any activities that you still find pleasure in or look forward to?

No... no, doctor, there's nothing. Absolutely nothing. It’s... it’s actually quite frightening how completely hollowed out everything has become. 

I used to have such a vibrant life, you know? My wife and I, we were always doing things. I used to spend whole afternoons at the art museum downtown—we had a membership, the one that lets you go to the special previews before the general public. I could spend hours just standing in front of a single impressionist painting, analyzing the brushstrokes, feeling this immense sense of connection to the history of it all. Or my photography... I had a whole darkroom set up in the basement at our old house, and even after we downsized, I bought this incredibly expensive digital camera. I used to wake up before dawn just to catch the perfect light over the lake. I was so passionate about it. And cooking! Oh, I used to love cooking for our friends. I’d spend two entire days preparing for a dinner party, making these elaborate French sauces from scratch, perfectly pairing the wines... 

But now? Now I look at that camera sitting on the shelf in my study, gathering dust, and I feel... absolutely nothing. Less than nothing, actually. I look at it and it just feels like a foreign object. My wife tried to get our bridge group back together last month, thinking it might help pull me out of this... this pit. They came over, and the table was set up, the cards were dealt, and I sat there looking at my hand, and the only thing I could feel was this crushing exhaustion at the sheer amount of effort it would take to just pretend. To pretend I cared about the bid, to pretend I cared about the conversation. I couldn't even fake a smile. I just excused myself and went back to my chair by the window. 

So, no. The museum, the camera, the bridge table, the kitchen... all of it is just gone. The joy has been completely drained out of everything, leaving just this awful, heavy emptiness. There isn't a single thing I look forward to anymore. Not one.
Have you experienced any breaks from reality, such as hallucinations or delusions, during these last nine months?

No... no, nothing like that. I mean, my mind is a terrible place to be right now, but it's... it's firmly planted in reality. Unfortunately. Sometimes I think it would be almost a relief if I were just imagining things, if this were all some sort of terrible dream or hallucination that I could wake up from. But no, the reality is exactly what I see. 

I haven't heard voices, if that's what you mean, or seen things that aren't there. I know some people experience that when they get very low, but for me, it's just the overwhelming presence of what *is* there. The silence in the house, the dust on my camera, the look of worry on my wife's face when she thinks I'm not looking. That's all very, very real. 

And delusions... well, no. Unless you count the absolute certainty that I've ruined everything, but that's not a delusion, doctor, that's just the cold, hard truth of the numbers. The bank statements aren't a delusion. The lost retirement funds aren't a delusion. It's all painfully, excruciatingly real. I sit in my study and I stare out the window, and I see the street, the neighbor's car, the mailman... it's all perfectly normal, perfectly mundane reality continuing on while my internal world has just... ended. So no, no breaks from reality. Just this one, unending, miserable reality that I can't escape.
Are there any small pleasures in life that you still enjoy, even if it's just for a moment?

Doctor... I know we touched on this a moment ago when you asked about things I look forward to, but the answer is still no. Not even for a moment. Not even the smallest thing. It's... it's all just ash in my mouth. 

I keep going back to how it used to be. I really do. I sit there and I try to remember what it felt like to enjoy a cup of coffee in the morning, or the feeling of satisfaction after making a really good meal. I mentioned the cooking, the French sauces... I used to find such immense pleasure in just the process of it, the chopping, the simmering, the way the house would smell. It was a small pleasure, yes, but it was profound. And the museum... just catching a glimpse of a certain color on a canvas could make my whole day. Or my photography. I’d spend hours waiting for the sun to hit the water just right, and when it did, that click of the shutter... it was a rush. A genuine, small, perfect moment of joy.

But now... I look at that expensive digital camera, the one I spent weeks researching before I bought it, and it's just a piece of metal and plastic. I feel absolutely nothing. There isn't even a flicker of interest. My wife tried to make my favorite meal last week—coq au vin, she used my recipe, she spent all afternoon on it—and I took one bite and it tasted like cardboard. I couldn't even appreciate the effort she put in, which just adds to the guilt, of course. 

And the bridge group... I told you about that. The cards were right there, the people I've known for twenty years were right there, laughing, trying to include me. And the only thing I felt... the *only* thing... was this monumental, crushing weight of the effort it would take to just pretend. To just fake a smile for five seconds. I couldn't do it. So, no, there are no small pleasures. There are no large pleasures. There is just this... this void where all of that used to be. It’s all gone.
Are you unable to experience pleasure from activities that you once found enjoyable?

Doctor, I... I know I keep coming back to this, and I apologize if I'm repeating myself, but yes. That is exactly what I'm trying to express. It's a complete and total inability. 

As I was just saying, I used to spend whole afternoons at the museum, just completely absorbed in the art, or I'd lose myself entirely in my photography and my cooking. I'd spend hours, literally hours, tweaking the exposure on a single photograph or reducing a sauce until it was absolutely perfect. It was my life, it was how I engaged with the world. 

But lately... lately I just look at my camera sitting there on the shelf, or I look at the bridge table when my wife tries to set it up, and I feel absolutely nothing. Nothing at all, except... except the sheer, exhausting effort it would take to just pretend. To pretend I still care about the f-stop on a lens, or whether someone bid two spades. It’s just... the capacity for it is completely gone. I sit in my chair by the window and I try to force myself to care, to just pick up the camera, just to hold it, but my arms feel like lead and my mind just refuses to engage. It's like the part of my brain that processed joy or interest has just been surgically removed. 

So, yes, to answer your question, I am completely unable to experience any pleasure from the things I used to love. It's all just dead to me now.
How long have you been feeling this low, with no pleasure in activities and overwhelming guilt?

Well, it's... it's been about nine months now. Nine months of this... this absolute wasteland. It started right after everything fell apart, all those grand plans I had, the financial ruin I brought on us. I can trace it back exactly to that point, to the day the realization really hit me that the money was gone and it was all my fault. 

Before that, I was... well, I was the opposite, wasn't I? I was full of energy, making all those investments, so sure of myself. But when it crashed down, it was like a switch was flipped. And since then, for these past nine months, it's just been this relentless, heavy, suffocating low. The guilt started immediately, of course. How could it not? Waking up every morning and remembering what I've done to our retirement, to my wife's security... it's the first thought in my head, and it just sets the tone for the entire day. 

And the loss of interest, the withdrawal... that followed right along with it. I stopped going to the museum within the first month. I couldn't bear to look at art when I felt so ugly inside. Then the camera went on the shelf. Then I stopped returning phone calls from the bridge group. My wife tried, she really did, she tried to keep me engaged those first few months, but... but I just retreated further and further into myself, into this chair by the window. 

So, yes, nine months. Nine months of sitting here, feeling guilty, feeling nothing else, just watching the seasons change outside the window while I'm completely frozen in this miserable state. It feels like a lifetime, doctor, it really does. I can barely remember what it felt like to be the man I was ten months ago. It's just been this continuous, unbroken stretch of darkness since those plans collapsed.
Would you describe your current episode of depression as mild, moderate, or severe?

Severe. Absolutely severe. I mean, I don't know how else to describe it, doctor. I sit here and I try to find a word that captures the sheer magnitude of this... this black hole that I'm trapped in, and 'severe' almost feels like an understatement, to be perfectly honest with you. 

I think about the word 'mild'—mild is a headache, mild is a rainy day when you wanted to go to the park. Moderate is maybe a bad flu, being stuck in bed for a week. But this? This is a complete and total obliteration of my life, of who I am. It's severe in every possible sense of the word. 

I wake up—if you can call it waking up, because I barely sleep, I just lie there churning over everything—and the physical weight of it is immediate. It's like someone has placed a lead blanket over my chest before I even open my eyes. The thought of just putting my feet on the floor, of standing up and facing another day of this endless nothingness, it's paralyzing. I spend hours just staring at the ceiling, trying to marshal the energy to swing my legs over the side of the bed. And when I finally do, what is there? There's my chair by the window. That's my entire world now. The distance from the bed to that chair feels like a marathon, and once I'm there, I just sit. I sit and I stare out at the street, watching people walk their dogs, watching the mailman, and I feel completely disconnected from the human race. 

It's severe because it's taken everything. It's taken my photography, my cooking, my friends, my ability to even converse with my wife without feeling like a burden. It's taken my dignity, doctor. I sit there in the same clothes for days because the effort of showering, of choosing a shirt, of buttoning buttons... it's insurmountable. I used to be a man who took pride in his appearance, you know? I wore a suit every day for forty years. And now I can't even manage to put on a clean pair of trousers. 

So yes, severe. It is a severe, crushing, all-consuming darkness that has completely swallowed me whole. I don't see any light at the end of the tunnel. I don't even see the tunnel anymore. I'm just buried under it all.
Have you experienced any symptoms like hearing voices or seeing things that aren't there during these last nine months?

No, no doctor. Nothing like that. I mean, my mind is... it's a terrible place to be right now, certainly, but it's not playing those kinds of tricks on me. I don't hear phantom voices or see visions or anything of that nature. The reality of what I've done is bad enough, I really don't need hallucinations to make it worse. 

When I sit in that chair by the window, the house is just... it's completely, suffocatingly quiet. The only voice I hear is my own. Just my own relentless internal monologue, going over and over the mistakes, the spreadsheets, the investments that wiped out our retirement. It's just me, constantly telling myself what an absolute fool I was. It's my own voice, just repeating the same accusations day in and day out. 

Sometimes the silence in that room is so heavy, you know? You sit there for hours and you just watch the dust motes floating in the gray light, and there's no one speaking, no visions, just the cold, hard reality of this mess I made. I almost think hearing a voice might be a distraction from the guilt, but no... my senses are perfectly intact, unfortunately. I see exactly what's in front of me, which is a ruined life, and I hear exactly what's there, which is just... dead silence. So, no, I haven't experienced anything like that at all. Just my own thoughts.
Has your current episode of depression lasted for more than two years?

Two years? Oh, no... no, no. As I... as I think I mentioned just a few moments ago, it's been about nine months. Nine months of this... this low, guilty withdrawal from everything and everyone. 

I mean, I can certainly understand why you might ask if it's been two years, because God knows it feels like it's been that long. It feels like a century, to be perfectly honest with you. When you're just sitting in the same chair by the window every single day, staring at the same patch of carpet, time just... it stops moving the way it's supposed to. An afternoon can feel like an entire lifetime when you have absolutely nothing to look forward to, and nothing but your own terrible regrets to keep you company. The days just bleed into one endless, gray stretch. 

But if we are looking strictly at the calendar... no, it hasn't been two years. It's been nine months since those plans fell apart. I know the timeline perfectly because I can trace it right back to the very week the investments collapsed and the reality of what I'd done to our retirement really hit me. That was the exact moment the bottom dropped out. Before that, I was so wrapped up in the spreadsheets and the grand ideas, but the second it all failed... that's when this unbearable guilt set in, and I just withdrew. I pulled away from my wife, from my friends, from life itself. 

So, no, not two years. Just these last nine agonizing months since the financial collapse. Though, I suppose when you're trapped at the bottom of a well, it doesn't really matter if you've been down there for nine months or two years, does it? The darkness looks exactly the same either way.
Would you say your current feelings of depression have been consistently severe over the past nine months?

Yes. Well, yes, absolutely consistent. Like I was just saying a moment ago, this... this low, guilty withdrawal has been going on for about nine months since those plans fell apart, and in all those days, in all those hundreds of days, there hasn't been a single break in the clouds. Not one. 

You hear about people having good days and bad days, don't you? Where maybe on a Tuesday they feel just terrible, but by Thursday they can at least muster a polite smile for the cashier at the grocery store, or they can actually taste their morning coffee. But for me? No. It has been a flat, unbroken line of absolute misery. From the very second I realized the money was gone, that my grand investment strategy was actually a complete and utter disaster... the severity of this feeling hasn't wavered for a fraction of a second. 

It doesn't take a day off. It doesn't lessen on weekends or holidays. My wife's birthday passed somewhere in month four or five, I think, and I couldn't even bring myself to sign a card, let alone take her out to dinner like we used to. The severity of it... it's just a constant, crushing pressure. I sit in that chair by the window, and the withdrawal from the world is just as deep today as it was in month one, or month three. If anything, I just retreat further and further inward, because the longer it goes on, the more the reality of what I've done settles into my bones. 

So when you ask if it's been consistently severe... yes, doctor. It is an unrelenting, every-single-minute kind of severe. Nine months of waking up and immediately remembering the ruin I've caused, and feeling that exact same lead blanket drop over my chest. There is no fluctuation. It never lets up. Not for a minute.

Severe. Absolutely severe. I mean, I don't know how else to describe it, doctor. I sit here and I try to find a word that captures the sheer magnitude of this... this black hole that I'm trapped in, and 'severe' almost feels like an understatement, to be perfectly honest with you. 

I think about the word 'mild'—mild is a headache, mild is a rainy day when you wanted to go to the park. Moderate is maybe a bad flu, being stuck in bed for a week. But this? This is a complete and total obliteration of my life, of who I am. It's severe in every possible sense of the word. 

I wake up—if you can call it waking up, because I barely sleep, I just lie there churning over everything—and the physical weight of it is immediate. It's like someone has placed a lead blanket over my chest before I even open my eyes. The thought of just putting my feet on the floor, of standing up and facing another day of this endless nothingness, it's paralyzing. I spend hours just staring at the ceiling, trying to marshal the energy to swing my legs over the side of the bed. And when I finally do, what is there? There's my chair by the window. That's my entire world now. The distance from the bed to that chair feels like a marathon, and once I'm there, I just sit. I sit and I stare out at the street, watching people walk their dogs, watching the mailman, and I feel completely disconnected from the human race. 

It's severe because it's taken everything. It's taken my photography, my cooking, my friends, my ability to even converse with my wife without feeling like a burden. It's taken my dignity, doctor. I sit there in the same clothes for days because the effort of showering, of choosing a shirt, of buttoning buttons... it's insurmountable. I used to be a man who took pride in his appearance, you know? I wore a suit every day for forty years. And now I can't even manage to put on a clean pair of trousers. 

So yes, severe. It is a severe, crushing, all-consuming darkness that has completely swallowed me whole. I don't see any light at the end of the tunnel. I don't even see the tunnel anymore. I'm just buried under it all.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychotic symptoms
doctor.question: Have you experienced any symptoms like hearing voices or seeing things that aren't there during these last nine months?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychotic symptoms such as hallucinations (hearing voices or seeing things), which are not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, no doctor. Nothing like that. I mean, my mind is... it's a terrible place to be right now, certainly, but it's not playing those kinds of tricks on me. I don't hear phantom voices or see visions or anything of that nature. The reality of what I've done is bad enough, I really don't need hallucinations to make it worse. 

When I sit in that chair by the window, the house is just... it's completely, suffocatingly quiet. The only voice I hear is my own. Just my own relentless internal monologue, going over and over the mistakes, the spreadsheets, the investments that wiped out our retirement. It's just me, constantly telling myself what an absolute fool I was. It's my own voice, just repeating the same accusations day in and day out. 

Sometimes the silence in that room is so heavy, you know? You sit there for hours and you just watch the dust motes floating in the gray light, and there's no one speaking, no visions, just the cold, hard reality of this mess I made. I almost think hearing a voice might be a distraction from the guilt, but no... my senses are perfectly intact, unfortunately. I see exactly what's in front of me, which is a ruined life, and I hear exactly what's there, which is just... dead silence. So, no, I haven't experienced anything like that at all. Just my own thoughts.

doctor.intent: Determine the duration of the patient's current depressive episode to differentiate between F33.1 and F33.2
doctor.question: Has your current episode of depression lasted for more than two years?

target_item.name: Depressive Episode Duration
target_item.manifestation: The low, guilty withdrawal has been going on for about nine months since those plans fell apart.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the current episode of depression has lasted for more than two years, which directly relates to the duration of the depressive episode.

patient.answer:
Two years? Oh, no... no, no. As I... as I think I mentioned just a few moments ago, it's been about nine months. Nine months of this... this low, guilty withdrawal from everything and everyone. 

I mean, I can certainly understand why you might ask if it's been two years, because God knows it feels like it's been that long. It feels like a century, to be perfectly honest with you. When you're just sitting in the same chair by the window every single day, staring at the same patch of carpet, time just... it stops moving the way it's supposed to. An afternoon can feel like an entire lifetime when you have absolutely nothing to look forward to, and nothing but your own terrible regrets to keep you company. The days just bleed into one endless, gray stretch. 

But if we are looking strictly at the calendar... no, it hasn't been two years. It's been nine months since those plans fell apart. I know the timeline perfectly because I can trace it right back to the very week the investments collapsed and the reality of what I'd done to our retirement really hit me. That was the exact moment the bottom dropped out. Before that, I was so wrapped up in the spreadsheets and the grand ideas, but the second it all failed... that's when this unbearable guilt set in, and I just withdrew. I pulled away from my wife, from my friends, from life itself. 

So, no, not two years. Just these last nine agonizing months since the financial collapse. Though, I suppose when you're trapped at the bottom of a well, it doesn't really matter if you've been down there for nine months or two years, does it? The darkness looks exactly the same either way.

doctor.intent: Determine the severity of the patient's depression to differentiate between F33.1 and F33.2
doctor.question: Would you say your current feelings of depression have been consistently severe over the past nine months?

target_item.name: Depressive Episode Duration
target_item.manifestation: The low, guilty withdrawal has been going on for about nine months since those plans fell apart.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the consistency and timeline of the depressive symptoms over the 9-month period, which corresponds to the depressive episode duration.

patient.answer:
Yes. Well, yes, absolutely consistent. Like I was just saying a moment ago, this... this low, guilty withdrawal has been going on for about nine months since those plans fell apart, and in all those days, in all those hundreds of days, there hasn't been a single break in the clouds. Not one. 

You hear about people having good days and bad days, don't you? Where maybe on a Tuesday they feel just terrible, but by Thursday they can at least muster a polite smile for the cashier at the grocery store, or they can actually taste their morning coffee. But for me? No. It has been a flat, unbroken line of absolute misery. From the very second I realized the money was gone, that my grand investment strategy was actually a complete and utter disaster... the severity of this feeling hasn't wavered for a fraction of a second. 

It doesn't take a day off. It doesn't lessen on weekends or holidays. My wife's birthday passed somewhere in month four or five, I think, and I couldn't even bring myself to sign a card, let alone take her out to dinner like we used to. The severity of it... it's just a constant, crushing pressure. I sit in that chair by the window, and the withdrawal from the world is just as deep today as it was in month one, or month three. If anything, I just retreat further and further inward, because the longer it goes on, the more the reality of what I've done settles into my bones. 

So when you ask if it's been consistently severe... yes, doctor. It is an unrelenting, every-single-minute kind of severe. Nine months of waking up and immediately remembering the ruin I've caused, and feeling that exact same lead blanket drop over my chest. There is no fluctuation. It never lets up. Not for a minute.
